catalog_quote: Isenye has only two tonal patterns, namely a H tone on the first syllable of the stem or a H tone linked to all syllables of the stem (7). The domain of the lexical tone is the nominal stem; noun class prefixes are toneless. Isenye nouns satisfies the stress-related criterion of obligatoriness (every word has at least one syllable with the highest prominence) but not culminativity, since multiply linked H (‘all H’) tones are allowed. Both H tones are aligned with the left edge of the stem, which can be viewed as a metrical restriction (Downing 2004). ... With this rather restricted tonal system it is possible that Isenye is changing from a tonal system towards a system with regular stress, possibly under the influence of the national language Swahili, which has regular penultimate stress. new_statements.quote: The Mara languages have previously been reported as accentual or “two type” languages with fairly reduced or non-existent lexical tonal contrasts (Bastin 2003). However, a closer look at the Mara languages shows that many have more than two lexical tonal contrasts and make use of melodic tones in their verbal systems. [...] It is worth mentioning that the varieties closest to Ikoma (Nata and Isenye) do not share the nominal tone system of Ikoma (Aunio 2015). The Nata nominal tone system is a stress system in which every noun can have only one stressed syllable, realised as a H tone [...] In Isenye, there are only two tone types for all noun stems: either there is a H tone on the first syllable of the noun stem or all the stem syllables are H.
new_statements.citation: Aunio, Lotta, Holly Robinson, Tim Roth, Oliver Stegen & John B. Walker. 2019. The Mara languages (JE40). In M. Van de Velde, K. Bostoen, D. Nurse & G. Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages, 2nd edn., 501-532. London: Routledge.
new_statements.locator: §2.3 Tone and syllable structure; Helda final-draft reprint pp. 7 and 10 of 29 (published pp. 501-532, draft pagination differs)
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog entry for Isenye has an empty rule. This chapter adds a positive characterization: tonal, two nominal tone types (stem-initial H or all-H), and explicitly contrasts Isenye with the Nata 'stress system', i.e. no word-stress rule is claimed for Isenye. Note: the listed open_url hdl:10138/309934 resolves to Crane 2019 'Totela K41' (wrong item, saved); the correct open copy is Helda hdl:10138/322322, which is what was downloaded and read.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Isenye is treated as a tone language (underlying H vs. toneless, at most one lexical H per morpheme in the family). For Isenye specifically the chapter states only that noun stems have two tone types, H on the stem-initial syllable or H on all stem syllables; it makes no statement about word stress for Isenye. Stress is mentioned only for neighbouring varieties: Nata is analysed as a one-H-per-word 'stress system' and some Zanaki speakers use regular penultimate stress.
new_statements.exceptions: none for Isenye; the chapter notes variation across Mara languages (Zanaki speakers split between tonal and penultimate-stress systems; Ngoreme weight-determined tone)
new_statements.identity_note: Isenye = Ishenyi (Laine 2023 spelling), a Western Serengeti / Mara (JE40) variety spoken between Ikoma and Nata in Tanzania; both works treat it as a variety distinct from Ikoma and Nata, not as a dialect of either. Aunio et al. 2019 is a family sketch of the Mara languages whose corpus languages are Ikoma, Ngoreme, Zanaki, Ikizu, Kabwa and Simbiti; Isenye is mentioned only in passing (nominal tone), so generalisations in the chapter about 'all six languages' do not cover Isenye.

new_statements.quote: Kuten suurin osa bantukielistä ja muista lähialueen kielistä, on isenjekin toonikieli. [...] Myöskään isenjen toonijärjestelmää ei ole vielä kattavasti tutkittu enkä käsittele sitä tässä työssä, mutta olen merkinnyt esimerkkien analysoimattomat pintatoonit näkyviin. [...] Isenjen kaikilla nominijuurilla on vain kaksi mahdollista toonia: joko juuren ensimmäisellä tai jokaisella tavulla on korkea tooni (Aunio 2015). [p. 42:] Sen sijaan penultima, joka tyypillisesti saa bantukielissä paljon prominenssia, ei isenjessä välttämättä pidenny.
new_statements.translation: Like most Bantu languages and the other languages of the surrounding area, Isenye too is a tone language. [...] Nor has the Isenye tone system yet been studied comprehensively, and I do not treat it in this work, but I have marked the unanalysed surface tones of the examples. [...] All Isenye nominal roots have only two possible tones: either the first syllable of the root or every syllable carries a high tone (Aunio 2015). [p. 42:] By contrast the penult, which in Bantu languages typically receives much prominence, does not necessarily lengthen in Isenye.
new_statements.citation: Laine, Antti. 2016. Isenjen kielen vokaalijarjestelma [The vowel system of Isenye]. MA thesis, University of Helsinki. ii+72 pp. hdl:10138/160466.
new_statements.locator: §1 introduction, pp. 2-3 (PDF pp. 6-7); §4.2 Vokaalin pituus, p. 42 (PDF p. 46)
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the empty catalog rule and with Aunio et al. 2019 (same two nominal tone patterns, both citing Aunio 2015). Adds the observation that penultimate lengthening/prominence is not systematic in Isenye. The Helda server throttled the PDF download
new_statements.rule_in_words: Isenye is a tone language whose tone system is not yet described; nominal roots have two tone patterns (root-initial H or all-H). No word-stress rule is given. The thesis adds that penultimate vowel lengthening, the usual Bantu correlate of penultimate prominence, is not obligatory in Isenye (vowel length is phonemic in roots; conditioned length comes from glide formation and prenasalisation, not from the penult).
new_statements.exceptions: none; the thesis explicitly excludes tone from its scope
new_statements.identity_note: Isenye = Ishenyi (Laine 2023 spelling), a Western Serengeti / Mara (JE40) variety spoken between Ikoma and Nata in Tanzania; both works treat it as a variety distinct from Ikoma and Nata, not as a dialect of either. Aunio et al. 2019 is a family sketch of the Mara languages whose corpus languages are Ikoma, Ngoreme, Zanaki, Ikizu, Kabwa and Simbiti; Isenye is mentioned only in passing (nominal tone), so generalisations in the chapter about 'all six languages' do not cover Isenye.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and domain quote are verbatim in the Aunio 2015 text we hold at the stated proof pages. (2) Deciding source is a 2015 peer-reviewed tone article by the principal fieldworker on these varieties; Glottolog's live bibliography (3 items) and Laine 2023's literature review show nothing better exists for Isenye prosody, and no instrumental or monograph-length phonology exists. (3) Laine 2023 (open, downloaded to independently restates the system as privative H/zero tone with syllable TBU, two nominal patterns in Ishenyi, toneless verb roots with melodic H, and attributes a stress analysis only to Nata, confirming tonal-OR-pitch accent for isse1238. Remaining unheld items (Aunio 2017, Aunio et al. 2019) are paywalled overviews by the same author and would at most refine the verbal-tone note. Identity: Isenye/I

sources.quote: 'Ws has a privative tone system (i.e. it can be analysed as having a distinction between h and (zero) tone ...), and the tone bearing unit is the syllable ... Ishenyi only has two nominal tonal patterns: a high tone on the first syllable of the stem, or on all stem syllables (Aunio 2015:5). Nata, on the other hand, can (and must) only have one high toned syllable per word, and is thus analysed as a stress system by Anghelescu (2012).' Also: 'Unlike nouns, verbs do not have lexical tonal contrasts. Verb roots are toneless, and infinitive forms have a melodic high tone on the first syllable of .
